item.title: An improved randomized algorithm for finding sinks of Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations of the binary hypercube
item.description: arXiv:2610.22546v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Acyclic Unique Sink Orientations (AUSOs) of the binary hypercube form an elegant abstraction of various optimization problems, ranging from linear programs whose feasibility region is a combinatorial hypercube, to 2-player turn-based stochastic games (2TBSGs) in which one of the players has two actions from each one of its states. The currently fastest known randomized algorithm for finding the sink of such AUSOs is the Random-Facet algorithm of Kalai (STOC 1992), and of Matou\v{s}ek, Sharir and Welzl (SoCG 1992), adapted to the binary hypercube by G\"{a}rtner (RSA 2002). The expected number of vertex queries made by the algorithm is at most $e^{2\sqrt{n}}$, where $n$ is the dimension of the cube. We design an improved randomized sink-finding algorithm that performs an expected number of only $e^{\sqrt{(2+o(1))n}}$ queries. This is the first improved bound for the problem in over two decades. The improved algorithm is obtained by adapting improved versions of the Random-Facet algorithm for solving general linear programs, and LP-type problems, developed by Kalai (STOC 1992), G\"{a}rtner (FOCS 1992), and by Hansen and Zwick (STOC 2015). The improved bound is not implied by these much more general algorithms. A key feature of the improved algorithm and its analysis is its simplicity. The structure of binary AUSOs enables a simpler description and a much simpler analysis of the adapted algorithm. In particular, the recurrence relations bounding the complexity of the algorithm depend on only one variable, and not two, and they can be solved using fairly straightforward techniques.
item.dc:creator: Thomas Dueholm Hansen, Uri Zwick

item.title: Hard Instances on Demand
item.description: arXiv:2610.22637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The conclusions of an experimental study of algorithms are only as good as the instances they are run on. Benchmark libraries for well-studied problems took decades to curate, while evaluations of new problems often fall back on random instances, which are known to be misleading: they may say more about the random generator than about the algorithmic question at hand. We treat instance generation as an optimization problem: parameterize the instance space, take the solver's running time as the objective, and let a black-box optimizer search for hard instances. We develop a widely applicable workflow built on the Nevergrad optimization platform and demonstrate it on four NP-hard problems: satisfiability, traveling salesperson, Hamiltonian cycle, and non-permutation flow-shop scheduling. The search needs only the solver, an instance encoder, and a compute budget. Our evolved instances beat the hardest instance of a budget-matched random draw in all four case studies, by an order of magnitude or more in three. They are often competitive with long-curated benchmark sets: our SAT champion is harder (for a three-solver portfolio) than 78% of the 498 SAT Competition formulas in its size class; our 20-city TSP champions take several times longer than the hardest measured classical TSPLIB instance (229 cities); and our flow-shop champion takes 238.6 seconds of CP Optimizer time to solve to proven optimality (versus 4.5 seconds for the hardest of 100,000 random draws) while denying CP-SAT an optimality proof. The optimizer even recovers known structure from running time alone: it locates a SAT clause/variable ratio near the phase transition and finds structurally different champions for the two scheduling engines.
item.dc:creator: Jamie Fravel, Martin Kouteck\'y, Pavlo Tsitsei

item.title: Improved Pass Complexity for Semi-Streaming Matching in General Graphs via Budgeted Price Approach
item.description: arXiv:2610.22718v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a simple deterministic semi-streaming algorithm that computes a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximate maximum matching in general graphs in $O(1/\varepsilon^{2})$ passes. This matches the pass complexity of the auction algorithm of Assadi, Liu, and Tarjan~[SOSA'21] for bipartite graphs, and answers Open Question~2 of Assadi~[SOSA'24 \& TheoretiCS'25]. Our approach, which we call the \emph{budgeted price approach}, is very different from the previous $\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)$-pass semi-streaming algorithms for $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation of matching in general graphs and improves their pass complexity. All previous approaches are augmenting-path-based and use $O(1/\varepsilon^{19})$ passes by Fischer, Mitrovi\'{c}, and Uitto~[STOC'22], $O(1/\varepsilon^{6})$ passes by Mitrovi\'{c}, Mukherjee, Sankowski, and Sheu~[ICALP'25], and $O(1/\varepsilon^{4})$ passes by Izumi, Kitamura, and Yamaguchi~['25].
item.dc:creator: Tatsuya Terao

item.title: Competitive Online Clustering with Movement Cost
item.description: arXiv:2610.22824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of online clustering with movement cost, which generalizes the fundamental $k$-server problem. At each time step, the algorithm is given a set of points in a metric space and must choose $k$ cluster centers. The cost incurred is the sum of the clustering cost at each time step and the total distance that the centers move over time. Prior work established competitive algorithms for the case $k\in\{1,2\}$ on the line metric with the $k$-median clustering objective; under the $k$-median objective, this problem is also known as facility reallocation. We substantially generalize these results to arbitrary $k$, general metric spaces, and a broad class of clustering objectives. Specifically, we consider clustering costs defined as a norm of the distance vector from points to their nearest center, which subsumes the $k$-median, $k$-center, and (square root of) $k$-means objectives, and provide an asymptotically optimal $O(k)$-competitive randomized algorithm against adaptive online adversaries. The algorithm is based on a reduction to the $k$-server problem, establishing a tight connection between the problems. In this reduction, $k$-server requests are generated by Poisson processes, whose arrival rates evolve in continuous time and are driven by a dual representation of the clustering costs. Our method of using Poissonization in this context may also be of independent interest. We demonstrate another use of the idea by deriving similar reductions for batched set chasing problems. We also consider a different family of clustering objectives defined as a norm of the vector of cluster radii, which subsumes the sum-$k$-radii and the $k$-center objectives, and give a tight $O(k)$-competitive deterministic algorithm on the line.
item.dc:creator: Christian Coester, Yichen Huang, Michael Mitzenmacher

item.title: On the Metric Distortion of the Minimum Spanning Tree Problem
item.description: arXiv:2610.23032v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the metric distortion of the minimum spanning tree (MST) problem when numerical edge weights are unavailable and each vertex reports only a ranking of the other vertices induced by these weights. We first show, through a simple example, that without assumptions on the weights, no ordinal algorithm guarantees a finite approximation ratio. We therefore focus on general metrics and present a Bor\r{u}vka-inspired algorithm using only ordinal comparisons that achieves distortion $O(\log n)$. We complement this result by showing that, for every $\varepsilon>0$, no deterministic ordinal algorithm guarantees distortion at most $3/2-\varepsilon$ on all finite metric instances. We then investigate more informative settings in pursuit of constant distortion, first considering two well-studied metric classes. For tree metrics realized on the given vertex set, a more careful variant of our initial algorithm achieves distortion~$1$, recovering an optimal MST from ordinal information alone. For the broad class of doubling metrics, a different algorithm based on \emph{endpoint cut stability} achieves distortion $2^{O(D)}$, where $D$ is the doubling dimension; this is constant for fixed $D$, independently of $n$. Finally, we study a query-based extension allowing comparisons between two edge lengths without revealing their numerical values. For general metrics with $n\geq2$, fewer than $n$ edge-comparison queries suffice to achieve distortion at most $2\log_2^* n-1$, which is near-constant even for very large inputs.
item.dc:creator: Kian Ghassemi, Masoud Seddighin, Saeed Seddighin

item.title: Online geometric matching and segments block points
item.description: arXiv:2610.23130v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a sequence of online points in general position in the plane, the geometric matching problem asks to match as many points as possible, subject to segment crossing constraints. We initiate the study of online geometric matching with limited crosses. In the $k$-crossing model each matched segment is allowed to have at most $k$ crosses, where $k=0$ corresponds to the online noncrossing matching model for which Bose et al. proved that Greedy is an optimal deterministic algorithm achieving a competitive ratio of $2/3$. In the triangle-free-crossing model no three matched segments are allowed to pairwise cross each other. Interestingly, we show in both cases the performance of Greedy does not improve by allowing crosses, and in fact, becomes worse in the $k$-crossing setting for $k\ge 1$. In the triangle-free-crossing model, we propose a simple two-layer-Greedy deterministic algorithm achieving a competitive ratio $4/5$. More interestingly, we propose and study the underlying segments blocking points extremal problem, and discuss its connection to vertex cover numbers and Ramsey numbers, with interesting open problems that might be of independent interest. We revisit the noncrossing model. We give a randomized algorithm which is an asymmetric version of Kamali et al., improving the competitive ratio from $0.66952$ to $0.67034$. We also show, via a conceptually simple construction, that no randomized algorithm can match more than $6/7$ fraction of points, improving the previous $16/17$ by Boyar et al.
item.dc:creator: Yaqiao Li, Junyi Lin

item.title: Critical-state algorithms for lot sizing with all-units discounts and variable inventory bounds
item.description: arXiv:2610.23253v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study deterministic single-item lot sizing with all-units quantity discounts, linear holding costs, and time-varying end-of-period inventory bounds. Unit prices may vary arbitrarily over time. For one common positive discount threshold, we give an exact algorithm requiring $O(n^3)$ arithmetic operations and $O(n^2)$ working space, including recovery of an optimal purchase plan. The method combines a critical-state theorem in cumulative-purchase coordinates with two prefix-minimum scans per dynamic-programming layer. The structural argument accommodates downward price discontinuities and distinguishes prescribed from free terminal inventory. With a fixed global set of $m$ positive threshold values, the bounds become $O_m(n^{m+2})$ time and $O_m(n^{m+1})$ space. Period-specific thresholds admit the same exact construction, but its state set can be exponential. For commensurate flow data, an inventory-lattice implementation takes $O(PW)$ time, where $P$ is the total number of price tiers and $W$ is the largest inventory-lattice width. We also derive a conditional optimality certificate from a monotone one-threshold relaxation; this certificate does not imply a near-linear worst-case algorithm for arbitrary prices. Exact-arithmetic implementations are checked against exhaustive inventory dynamic programs and tier-enumeration linear programs. An illustrative timing study identifies settings in which the lattice implementation is preferable.
item.dc:creator: Kleitos Papadopoulos

item.title: Simpler Algorithms for Capacitated $k$-Median with $(1 + \epsilon)$-Violations Using New Inequalities
item.description: arXiv:2610.23348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We revisit the capacitated $k$-median problem, focusing on constant-factor approximation algorithms with either $(1+\epsilon)$-cardinality or capacity violations. Previous results [DemirciL16, Li16} achieve an $O_\epsilon(1)$-approximation with $(1+\epsilon)$-violations via complex extended configuration linear programming formulations with the round-or-cut framework. We propose a simpler, unified round-or-cut framework that handles both cardinality and capacity violation settings. Our main technical contribution is a mechanism that directly utilizes the costs of local instances to generate valid inequalities. Specifically, we partition the metric space into local pieces of size $O(1/\epsilon)$ as in previous work, and construct instances of capacitated clustering with penalties, which allow client demands to be unserved at a penalty cost. Solving these local instances yields lower bounds on the original LP cost, yielding valid LP constraints. In contrast, previous approaches rely on complex extended configuration LPs over connection variables $x_{ij}$'s and opening variables $y_i$'s. As a secondary contribution, our approach achieves an improved running time of $\text{poly}(n, 1/\epsilon)$, bypassing the exponential dependence on $1/\epsilon$ required to solve the previous extended configuration LPs. Instead of solving the local instances optimally in time exponential in $1/\epsilon$, we obtain $O(1/\epsilon)$-approximate solutions in $\text{poly}(n, 1/\epsilon)$ time. Finally, for the cardinality-violation setting, our algorithm opens a set of at most $(1+\epsilon)k$ $\textit{distinct}$ facilities, and thus gives a bicriteria approximation in the $\textit{hard-capacitated}$ setting. In contrast, the algorithm of [Li16] may open the same facility multiple times.
item.dc:creator: Han Dai, Shi Li

item.title: Power of Conditional Sampling on Hypergraphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.23364v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Let $G=(V,E)$ be a $d$-uniform hypergraph with $|V|=n$ and $|E|=m$. Estimating $m$ from uniformly random hyperedge samples requires $\Theta(\sqrt{m})$ samples by a birthday-paradox argument. We investigate the power of conditional sampling through a hierarchy of oracles: for an integer $1\le s\le d$, given pairwise disjoint subsets $X_1,\ldots,X_s\subseteq V$, the $s$-colorful oracle returns a hyperedge chosen uniformly at random from all hyperedges contained in $X_1\cup\cdots\cup X_s$ that intersect every $X_i$, provided one exists. For $s=1$, this samples a uniformly random hyperedge induced by $X_1$. For every $1\le s\le d$, we give a randomized algorithm that outputs $\widehat{m}\in[(1-\varepsilon)m,(1+\varepsilon)m]$ with probability at least $2/3$ using $O_{s,d}(\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n))$ conditional samples, where the exponent of $\log n$ is an absolute constant independent of both $s$ and $d$. Conditional sampling thus yields an exponential separation over uniform hyperedge sampling. We also study the decision version, in which the oracle only reports whether a qualifying hyperedge exists. For every $1\le s<d$, we prove that any algorithm using the $s$-colorful decision oracle requires $\widetilde{\Omega}_{s,d}(n^{\frac{d-s}{d-s+1}})$ queries. Hence, for $s<d$, access to uniformly random witness hyperedges (random certificates) is exponentially more powerful than existence queries. For $s=d$, decision queries alone achieve $\operatorname{poly}(1/\varepsilon,\log n)$ query complexity, but the exponent of $\log n$ is known to be $\Theta(d)$. The colorful hierarchy thus exhibits a phase transition at $s=d$: for $s<d$, random certificates are essential for polylogarithmic-query estimation, whereas at $s=d$ decision queries suffice, yet random certificates still provably reduce the exponent of $\log n$ from $\Theta(d)$ to an absolute constant.
item.dc:creator: Debarshi Chanda, Buddha Dev Das, Arijit Ghosh, Gopinath Mishra

item.title: Deterministic Global Minimum Cut Using $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ Cut Queries
item.description: arXiv:2610.23461v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finding a global minimum cut in an unweighted graph is a fundamental task in the cut-query model. While there exists a randomized algorithm for this task using $\tilde O(n)$ queries, known deterministic algorithms use $\tilde{O}(n^{5/3})$ queries. We improve upon this result and give a simple deterministic algorithm that finds a global minimum cut using $\tilde O(\min\left\{ n\delta,n^2/\delta \right\})$ cut queries, which equals $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ in the worst case, where $\delta$ is the minimum degree of the graph. The key ingredient in our approach is an efficient maximum $s,t$-flow algorithm, for the case when the minimum $s,t$-cut has value at most $\delta$.
item.dc:creator: Yotam Kenneth-Mordoch

item.title: Approximating the Girth of an Undirected, Weighted Graph for Larger Approximation Factors
item.description: arXiv:2610.23698v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The girth of a weighted undirected graph is defined as the length of a shortest cycle in the graph. In this paper, we give a randomized $O\left(m^{1+2/(k-1)} n^{1/(k-1)}\right)$ algorithm to approximate the girth of a graph with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges to within a factor of $k$ for any real $k$. We assume that all edge weights are non-negative. For sufficiently high approximation factors, our algorithm outperforms the state of the art by polylogarithmic factors. Specifically, for approximation factors $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ where $c>5$, our algorithm gives a runtime of $O\left(m (\log n)^{5/c}\right)$, while instantiating the previous best $k$-approximation algorithms with $k = c\frac{\log n}{\log \log n}$ yields a running time of $O\left( \frac{cn (\log n)^{2 + 4/(3c)} }{\log \log n} + m\log n\right)$ (Kadria, Roditty, and Vassilevska Williams, arXiv:2607.00938). Furthermore, the algorithm presented here is conceptually simple, has relatively small constants, eschews single-source shortest path and sparse spanner algorithms, and employs a new technique, which we call ``random filtering.'' That being said, the basic algorithm returns only a numerical estimate for the girth, rather than a witness cycle.
item.dc:creator: Eliyahu Yablon

item.title: Dynamic Load Balancing under Restricting Updates
item.description: arXiv:2610.23768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of load balancing in the dynamic setting. The input is a bipartite graph $G = (J \cup M, E)$ of jobs $J$ and machines $M$. Every job has a positive weight $w(j)$. The goal is to assign every job in $J$ to an adjacent machine in $M$ so as to minimize the maximum machine load, where the load of a machine is the sum of the weights of the jobs assigned to it. Although load balancing has been studied extensively in many models of computation, the only previous result in the dynamic model addresses the \emph{incremental} setting, where updates take the form of edge insertions and job deletions [BKS23b]. The authors show a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximation for incremental \emph{fractional} load balancing with $\text{poly}(\log(n),1/\epsilon)$ update time; they point out that their techniques do not extend to the decremental setting. Main Result: We obtain an algorithm which maintains a $(1+\epsilon)$-approximate solution to the fractional load balancing problem under edge deletions and job insertions in $\tilde{O}(\log (n), 1/\epsilon)$ update time. Our techniques are very different from those of the incremental algorithm of [BKS23b]. Instead, our algorithm is inspired by a load-balancing algorithm from the {\sc congest} model of computation [ALPZ21]. We develop a novel analytic framework for this algorithm, which allows us to show that it performs well in the dynamic setting. Rounding Scheme: We also present a black-box rounding scheme for dynamic load balancing. Plugging in our fractional algorithm, we obtain a decremental algorithm for $(2+\epsilon)$-approximate \emph{integral} load balancing with $\text{poly}(\log(n),1/\epsilon)$ update time. We also obtain the same bounds for incremental load balancing by plugging in the fractional algorithm of [BKS23b].
item.dc:creator: Aaron Bernstein, Sayan Bhattacharya, Peter Kiss, Thatchaphol Saranurak

item.title: Polytope Sampling at the Speed of Isoperimetry
item.description: arXiv:2610.23775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give faster algorithms for sampling from the uniform distribution over a polytope. Our main result is an algorithm that, when applied to a polytope with $m$ constraints in $n$ dimensions, uses $m \cdot \mathrm{poly}\log(\frac m \delta)$ iterations, each running in time $O(mn^{\omega - 1})$, to return a sample within total variation distance $\delta$ to the uniform distribution. When $m =O(n)$ and $\delta = \mathrm{poly}(\frac 1 n)$, our runtime improves upon all prior works by an $\Omega(n^{2/3})$ factor. Our sampler is based on the recent \emph{functional stochastic localization} framework of [GST26], and achieves an iteration count nearly matching the Poincar\'e constant of the uniform distribution with respect to the logarithmic barrier.
item.dc:creator: Anming Gu, Bobby Shi, Kevin Tian, Hubert Yang

item.title: Online Graph Coloring with Random Arrivals
item.description: arXiv:2610.23824v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study online graph coloring in the random-arrival model, where the vertices are presented in a uniformly random order. Assuming $n$ and $k$ are known in advance, we present a randomized exponential-time algorithm that colors any $k$-colorable graph on $n$ vertices with $O(k^3 \log^2 k \log^4 n)$ colors in expectation. This is the first online coloring algorithm that uses a polylogarithmic number of colors for all fixed $k \geq 3$, and is better than a known lower bound of $\Omega(\log^{k-1} n)$ colors under adversarial arrivals for all fixed $k \geq 6$. In addition, assuming $n$ is known in advance, we obtain a competitive ratio of $\widetilde{O}(n^{2/3})$. For comparison, it is known to be NP-hard to approximate (offline) graph coloring within a factor of $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ for all fixed $\varepsilon > 0$. Therefore, our exponential-time online algorithm achieves a performance guarantee beyond the NP-hardness threshold for polynomial-time approximation algorithms.
item.dc:creator: Hirotaka Yoneda, Masataka Yoneda

item.title: Computing bounded solutions to linear Diophantine equations with the sum of divisors
item.description: arXiv:2601.17832v2 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We propose an efficient computational method for finding all solutions $n\leq U$ to the Diophantine equation $a\sigma(n)=bn+c$, where $a,b,c$ are fixed integer coefficients, $U$ is a given upper bound, and $\sigma(n)$ denotes the sum of divisors of $n$. The method combines advanced pruning of possible prime factors of $n$ and their combinations with several optimization techniques, organized around a \emph{prime-wheel} data structure developed for this purpose. It is implemented in the {\sc SageMath} computer algebra system within the framework of recursively enumerated sets and supports native {\sc MapReduce} parallelization. We apply the method to numerous previously studied equations, discovering new solutions, certifying complete solution lists below substantially larger bounds than previously reported, and substantially improving lower bounds in several open problems involving the sum-of-divisors function.
item.dc:creator: Max A. Alekseyev

item.title: Fast Distributed $(\Delta + 1)$-Edge Coloring in Bipartite Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.22690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that, on bipartite $n$-vertex graphs in the LOCAL model of distributed computation, $(\Delta + 1)$-edge coloring can be solved deterministically in $O(f(\Delta) \log n)$ rounds for some function $f$. In particular this implies a deterministic $O(\log n)$-round upper bound for $(\Delta + 1)$-edge coloring on bipartite constant-degree graphs. Our results improve on the previous state-of-the-art bounds (which hold already on general graphs) whose $n$-dependencies are $\widetilde{O}(\log^5 n)$ rounds deterministically and $\widetilde{O}(\log^2 n)$ rounds randomized [Bernshteyn and Dhawan, J.\ Comb.\ Theory 2025]. In fact, we obtain the aforementioned results already for a more restrictive version of $(\Delta + 1)$-edge coloring that corresponds to a \emph{local-palette} strengthening of Vizing's theorem shown recently to hold [Christiansen, STOC 2023]. In this version, every edge $\{u, v\}$ has to be colored with a color from $\{1, \dots, \max(\operatorname{deg}(u), \operatorname{deg}(v))+ 1\}$. For all of our results, the vertices do not need to know on which side of the bipartition they lie---the structural promise of bipartiteness suffices.
item.dc:creator: Yann Bourreau, Sebastian Brandt, Ananth Narayanan

item.title: Peak-Memory Schedules You Can Trust: Exact Realization, Certified Optimality, and the Limits of Recomputation for Inference
item.description: arXiv:2610.23328v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-time inference on small devices needs low activation memory without extra latency, which makes operator order the most valuable memory lever: it is free in time. We show that the usual way of deploying a better order, handing it back to the compiler and regenerating code, is unreliable. In PyTorch Inductor the regenerated program misses its predicted peak in 22 of 54 CPU configurations. It is worse than the stock program in 9 of them and in 19 of 50 on a GPU, and on the GPU it also changes numerical results. We instead profile the generated program, model its memory exactly from its own statements and their read/write effects, and permute those statements. We prove that this realizes the modeled peak whenever allocation does not depend on history. It does so to the byte, with bitwise-identical results, in all our CPU runs. On the GPU we characterize why the caching allocator breaks the condition. To know when to stop, we give forward and reverse "trap" lower bounds, each computable with $O(n^2)$ minimum cuts. They certify the found order optimal for 94% of held-out wrapper graphs and all 16 microcontroller-class models we study, in under a second. So most inference graphs are already scheduled optimally. Branching networks are the exception, where reordering is free and pays, e.g. 10.0% on DeepLabV3. In compiled training we save up to 7.6%. Beyond the certified optimum we study selective recomputation with per-operator caps. It is strongly NP-hard for every fixed cap even at treewidth two, encodes knapsack exactly on series-parallel graphs, and is solvable exactly on bounded treewidth. It is useless on public tiny models whose peak is a single layer, but on architectures that hold a cheap value for a late reuse it pays: on the public ReDimNet speaker networks, whose order is already optimal, it lowers the peak by 5.2-6.1% at under 0.4% extra MACs, with bitwise-identical outputs.
item.dc:creator: Ivan Fomin, Ivan Koryabkin, Boris Sheludko

item.title: Rapid mixing within a phase for Ising models
item.description: arXiv:2610.23777v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We study Glauber dynamics for Ising measures conditioned to have a sufficiently large majority of $+1$ spins. Under a sparse spectral width condition on the interaction matrix, we derive a Poincar\'{e} inequality for the conditioned measures from a magnetization drift condition, and a modified logarithmic Sobolev inequality from a stronger, entropy weighted condition. As applications, we obtain approximate posterior sampling in total variation distance for $\mathbb{Z}_2$ synchronization at high enough signal-to-noise ratio using $O(n\log n)$ Glauber updates from a spectral initialization. For ferromagnetic Ising models on random $d$-regular graphs, we prove rapid phase ordering down to inverse temperatures of order $1/d$, extending the temperature range of Gheissari, Sly, and Sohn (2025). Finally, we extend these inequalities to unconditioned Ising measures under an inward drift condition outside the conditioned region. This yields $O(n\log n)$ mixing of Glauber dynamics for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at every fixed inverse temperature when the external field is sufficiently large.
item.dc:creator: Vasyl Paliy, Youngtak Sohn

item.title: Recognizing 2-Layer and Outer $k$-Planar Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2412.04042v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The crossing number of a graph is the least number of crossings over all drawings of the graph in the plane. Computing the crossing number of a given graph is NP-hard, but fixed-parameter tractable (FPT) with respect to the natural parameter. Two well-known variants of the problem are 2-layer crossing minimization and circular crossing minimization, where every vertex must lie on one of two layers, namely two parallel lines, or a circle, respectively. Both variants are NP-hard, but FPT with respect to the natural parameter. Recently, a local version of the crossing number has also received considerable attention. A graph is $k$-planar if it admits a drawing with at most $k$ crossings per edge. In contrast to the crossing number, recognizing $k$-planar graphs is NP-hard even if $k=1$. In this paper, we consider the two above variants in the local setting. The $k$-planar graphs that admit a straight-line drawing with vertices on two layers or on a circle are called 2-layer $k$-planar and outer $k$-planar graphs, respectively. We study the parameterized complexity of the two recognition problems with respect to $k$. For $k=0$, both problems can easily be solved in linear time. Two groups independently showed that outer 1-planar graphs can also be recognized in linear time [Hong et al., Algorithmica 2015; Auer et al., Algorithmica 2016]. One group asked whether outer 2-planar graphs can be recognized in polynomial time. Our main contribution consists of XP-algorithms for recognizing 2-layer $k$-planar graphs and outer $k$-planar graphs. We complement these results by showing that both recognition problems are XNLP-hard. This implies that both problems are W$[t]$-hard for every $t$ and that it is unlikely that they admit FPT-algorithms. On the other hand, we present an FPT-algorithm for recognizing 2-layer $k$-planar graphs where the order of the vertices on one layer is specified.
item.dc:creator: Yasuaki Kobayashi, Yuto Okada, Alexander Wolff

item.title: Dynamic Graph Coloring: Sequential, Parallel, and Distributed
item.description: arXiv:2512.09218v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We present a simple randomized algorithm that can efficiently maintain a $(\Delta+1)$ coloring as the graph undergoes edge insertion and deletion updates, where $\Delta$ denotes an upper bound on the maximum degree. A key advantage is the algorithm's ability to process many updates simultaneously, which makes it naturally adaptable to parallel and distributed computations. Concretely, it gives a unified framework across the models, leading to the following results: - In the sequential setting, the algorithm processes each update in $O(1)$ expected time, worst-case. This matches and strengthens the results of Henzinger and Peng [TALG 2022] and Bhattacharya et al. [TALG 2022], who achieved an $O(1)$ bound but amortized over the sequence of updates (in expectation and with high probability, respectively), whose work improved the $O(\log \Delta)$ expected amortized bound of Bhattacharya et al. [SODA'18]. - In the parallel setting, the algorithm processes each batch of updates using $O(1)$ work per update in the batch in expectation, and in $\text{poly}(\log n)$ depth with high probability. This is, in a sense, an ideal parallelization of the above results. - In the distributed setting, the algorithm can maintain a coloring of the network graph as (potentially many) edges are added or deleted. The maintained coloring is always proper; it may become partial upon updates, i.e., some nodes may temporarily lose their colors, but quickly converges to a full, proper coloring. Concretely, each insertion and deletion causes at most $O(1)$ nodes to become uncolored, but this is resolved within $\tilde{O}(\log n)$ rounds with high probability (e.g., in the absence of further updates nearby--the precise guarantee is stronger, but technical). Importantly, the algorithm incurs only $O(1)$ expected message complexity and computation per update.
item.dc:creator: Mohsen Ghaffari, Jaehyun Koo

item.title: A simple $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation for knapsack interdiction
item.description: arXiv:2604.21877v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the knapsack interdiction problem, there are $n$ items, each with a non-negative profit, interdiction cost, and packing weight. There is also an interdiction budget and a capacity. The objective is to select a set of items to interdict (delete) subject to the budget which minimizes the maximum profit attainable by packing the remaining items subject to the capacity. We present a $(2+\epsilon)$-approximation running in $O(n^3\epsilon^{-1}\log(\epsilon^{-1}\log\sum_i p_i))$ time, where $p_i$ is the profit of item $i$. Although a polynomial-time approximation scheme (PTAS) is already known for this problem, our algorithm is considerably simpler and faster. The approach also generalizes naturally to a $(1+t+\epsilon)$-approximation for $t$-dimensional knapsack interdiction with running time $O(n^{t+2}\epsilon^{-1}\log(\epsilon^{-1}\log\sum_i p_i))$. In computational experiments on standard benchmark instances with $\epsilon=1$, our algorithm is on average within 0.4% of optimal and over 20 times faster than a state-of-the-art exact algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Noah Weninger

item.title: A Complexity Dichotomy for Edge Subdivision to $H$-Free Graphs
item.description: arXiv:2604.24228v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: For a fixed graph $H$, \HFS\ asks whether at most $k$ edge subdivisions can make an input graph contain no induced copy of $H$. We establish a complexity dichotomy for every fixed nonempty $H$: the problem is polynomial-time solvable if every component of $H$ is a subdivided star or a subdivided bistar and at most one component is a subdivided bistar; it is NP-complete otherwise. In every NP-complete case, the Exponential Time Hypothesis rules out a $2^{o(k)}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm. For every fixed $H$, the problem admits a $2^{O(k)}n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm.
item.dc:creator: Marta Piecyk, R. B. Sandeep

item.title: Fully Dynamic Edge Connectivity in $\tilde{O}(n^{12/13})$ Time
item.description: arXiv:2607.10689v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In the (fully) dynamic edge connectivity problem, the goal is to maintain the edge connectivity $\lambda_G$ of an $n$-vertex graph $G$ that undergoes edge insertions and deletions. Our main result is a randomized algorithm for maintaining edge connectivity in dynamic simple graphs using worst-case update and query time $\tilde{O}(n^{12/13})$, for all values of $\lambda_G$. This is the first algorithm that has $o(n)$ update and query time, as all existing algorithms achieve this only when $\lambda_G$ is below $n^{1/11}$ or above $n^{1/2}$ (up to polylogarithmic factors). We then use the tools developed for this purpose to design two additional algorithms. The first one is a deterministic algorithm for the exact same task, that uses $n^{1+o(1)}$ worst-case update and query time or $\tilde{O}(n)$ amortized update and query time; this gives a polynomial improvement over existing deterministic algorithms. The second one is a deterministic algorithm for the same task but in dynamic unweighted multigraphs, that uses $\tilde{O}(n^{3/2})$ worst-case update and query time.
item.dc:creator: Yotam Kenneth-Mordoch, Robert Krauthgamer

item.title: An $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$-time FPRAS for the Permanent
item.description: arXiv:2609.20717v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give an FPRAS for the permanent of an $n\times n$ $0/1$ matrix with running time $\widetilde O(n^3)$. Our algorithm extends to a strongly polynomial FPRAS for arbitrary nonnegative matrices with the same running-time bound (but in the unit-cost arithmetic model). Jerrum, Sinclair, and Vigoda (2004) gave the first FPRAS for the permanent of a nonnegative matrix. The running time was subsequently improved to $\widetilde{O}(n^7)$ by Bez\'akov\'a, \v{S}tefankovi\v{c}, Vazirani, and Vigoda (2008), and recently to $\widetilde{O}(n^6)$ by Chen, Vigoda, and Yang (2026). We introduce a multicommodity-flow bound inspired by electrical flows, replacing the usual path-length factor by routing energy. For the classical JSV chain with perfect-matching weights multiplied by $n^2$, we prove a relaxation-time bound of $O(n^3\log n)$ and obtain comparable bounds for estimating the stationary probabilities of having a specified pair of unmatched vertices. We use a separate chain on assignments to generate a warm start at any given temperature, avoiding the long initialization of the JSV chain. Finally, we replace the JSV chain with a new chain that uses only $n$ hole weights and speeds up hole-weight learning by a factor of $n$.
item.dc:creator: Xiaoyu Chen, Heng Guo, Eric Vigoda, Xiongxin Yang

item.title: Breaking the $2^n$ barrier for directed hamiltonicity
item.description: arXiv:2609.39062v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a randomized algorithm for Directed Hamiltonian Cycle on $n$-vertex directed graphs that runs in $O^*(1.9133^n)$ time. For general directed graphs, this is the first improvement in the exponential base over the classical $O(2^n n^2)$-time algorithms of Bellman and Held--Karp (1962). To obtain this improvement, we reduce Hamiltonicity to weighted parity counting using the isolation lemma of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (STOC 1987). If a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$ exists, assigning random polynomially bounded integer weights to the arcs gives a unique minimum-weight Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$ with constant probability. In particular, the path count at its total weight is odd. To compute these parities, we give a $(2-2^{-d})^n n^{O(1)}$-time algorithm for instances in which the arcs entering each vertex have at most $d$ distinct polynomially bounded integer weights. The algorithm applies the random linearization idea of Arvind and Guruswami (IPEC 2021) to the Laplacian determinant construction of Bj\"orklund, Kaski, and Koutis (ICALP 2017). To keep $d$ small, we randomly delete and duplicate arcs and partition the incoming copies at each vertex into $d$ groups, assigning a common weight to all arcs in each group. We prove that, if the input graph has a Hamiltonian path from $s$ to $t$, then with positive, albeit exponentially small, probability one can select one group at each vertex so that their union contains an odd number of such paths.
item.dc:creator: Tomohiro Koana, Soh Kumabe

item.title: A deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs
item.description: arXiv:2610.09972v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for the Bilu--Linial signing problem on bipartite graphs. For every finite simple bipartite graph of maximum degree at most an integer $\Delta\ge3$, the algorithm assigns signs to its edges so that the signed adjacency matrix has operator norm strictly less than $2\sqrt{\Delta-1}$. Our algorithm builds on the randomized recursive repair framework of Jadbabaie, Saberi, and Sra~\cite{JSS26}, with deterministic rules for sign selection and vertex deletion.
item.dc:creator: Zhiqiang Xu

item.title: Subset Sum and Integer Programming Feasibility Test in Near-Optimal Time
item.description: arXiv:2610.12953v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We give an $O_{d,\varepsilon}(n+N^{d+\varepsilon})$-time algorithm for multidimensional subset sum on an explicitly listed multiset of $n$ vectors in $[-N,N]^d$, for every fixed $d$ and $\varepsilon>0$. This directly implies an $O_{d,\varepsilon}(n+N^{d+\varepsilon})$-time algorithm for feasibility test of integer programming. Prior to our work, the best-known algorithm has a running time of $O_{d}(n+N^{O(d^2)})$ [Eisenbrand, Weismantel'19]. Specifically, if $d=1$, our algorithm runs in $O_{\varepsilon}(n+N^{1+\varepsilon})$-time for the standard subset sum problem, which is near-linear in the largest input integer. Prior to our work, subset sum can be solved in time near-linear in the target $t$ [Bringmann'17], or near-linear in the mixed parameter $\sqrt{Nt}$ [Chen, Lian, Mao, Zhang'24]. It is a fundamental open problem whether the algorithm can be made near-linear in $N$, which is settled affirmatively in this paper up to an arbitrary small $N^{\varepsilon}$ term.
item.dc:creator: Lin Chen, Yuchen Mao, Guochuan Zhang

item.title: Inclusion-wise extremal knapsack problems are (mostly) hard to approximate
item.description: arXiv:2610.18017v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: We study two inclusion-wise extremal variants of the 0-1 Knapsack Problem (KP). Given $n$ items with integer weights and nonnegative costs or profits, the Minimum-Cost Maximal Knapsack Packing Problem seeks a minimum-cost packing for capacity $c$ to which no item can be added, while the Maximum-Profit Minimal Knapsack Cover Problem seeks a maximum-profit cover for threshold $d$ from which no item can be removed. Both problems are weakly $\mathrm{NP}$-hard and pseudo-polynomially solvable, as is the classical KP, but their approximability is fundamentally different: unless $\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}$, with positive values neither problem admits a polynomial-time $2^{p(n)}$-approximation for any polynomial $p$; allowing zero values rules out every multiplicative factor. Even with unit costs for packing and unit profits for covering, neither admits an $n^{1-\varepsilon}$-approximation for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$, whereas a trivial $n$-approximation exists. We identify restrictions that restore approximability. If every item weighs at least a fixed fraction of the capacity, respectively of the threshold, both problems can be solved exactly in polynomial time. For the cover problem, if each weight $w_i$ satisfies $w_i-1\ge\delta(d-1)$, we give an approximation scheme for arbitrary profits whose running time is polynomial in $n$, $1/\varepsilon$, and $1/\delta$. If values equal weights, a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme (FPTAS) was already known for the packing problem; we give an FPTAS for the cover problem, improving on the previously known factor $2$. If value-to-weight ratios differ by at most a factor $\kappa$, we obtain a $(1+\varepsilon)\kappa$-approximation for both problems.
item.dc:creator: Fabio Ciccarelli, Fabio Furini, Ulrich Pferschy, Elena Rener

item.title: The Complexity of Hamiltonian Cycles and Paths with Prescribed Walk Lengths
item.description: arXiv:2610.18300v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Fix a set $S$ of positive integers. An $S$-Hamiltonian cycle is a cyclic ordering of all vertices of a graph such that each consecutive pair is joined by a walk whose length belongs to $S$. We study the complexity of deciding whether an input graph admits such an ordering, together with the corresponding path variants with prescribed or unrestricted endpoints. We complete the complexity classification for undirected graphs. In particular, we prove NP-completeness for every finite nonempty set of odd lengths, resolving an open problem posed by Amarilli, Lombardo, and Monet (WG 2026). For digraphs, all three problems are NP-complete for every fixed finite nonempty $S$ and admit linear-time algorithms when $S$ is cofinite. For other fixed infinite sets $S$, we establish NP-complete and undecidable cases, with undecidability occurring even when $S$ is recursive.
item.dc:creator: Hitendra Kumar, Mathieu Mari, R. B. Sandeep

item.title: Hypothesis Selection via Weighted Medians
item.description: arXiv:2610.20375v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Given $n$ distributions (hypotheses) $\mathcal H=\{H_1,\ldots,H_n\}$ and samples from an unknown target distribution $P$, proper hypothesis selection seeks a distribution whose total variation distance to $P$ is close to the best achievable within the known distributions. We give an algorithm that, using $O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ target samples, running in $O(n\varepsilon^{-2}\log(n/\delta))$ time, with probability at least $1-\delta$, returns $H_{\hat i}$ satisfying $d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_{\hat i})\leq 3\min_{i\in[n]}d_\mathrm{TV}(P,H_i)+\varepsilon.$ The algorithm achieves the optimal approximation factor and sample complexity. The running time improves the dependence on the failure probability from polynomial to logarithmic in the state-of-the-art bound $\tilde{O}(n\varepsilon^{-2}\delta^{-1})$ of Aamand, Aliakbarpour, Chen, and Silwal (COLT 2026), thereby answering their Question~2.
item.dc:creator: Liang-Yu Zou

item.title: Best-of-Both-Worlds Guarantees with Fairer Endings
item.description: arXiv:2507.16209v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We study best-of-both-worlds guarantees for the fair division of indivisible goods. Prior work has shown that under additive valuations, there always exists a randomized allocation that is ex-ante stochastic-dominance envy-free (sd-EF) and ex-post envy-free up to one good (EF1). Our work is motivated by the goal of achieving stronger ex-post fairness guarantees such as envy-freeness up to any good (EFX). Towards this goal, we make the following contributions: (i) Our first set of results considers a subdomain of additive valuations called \textit{lexicographic} preferences. On the negative side, we show that ex-ante sd-EF is fundamentally in conflict with ex-post EFX, prompting a relaxation in the ex-ante benchmark. On the positive side, we present a polynomial time algorithm that achieves ex-ante $\max\{1-\frac{2}{n+1},\,\frac{9}{10}\}$-EF and ex-post EFX and Pareto optimality, where $n$ is the number of agents. Our algorithm uses a novel dependent rounding technique that, to the best of our knowledge, is its first application in fair division. (ii) Our second set of results concerns beyond-additive valuations. We present a pseudopolynomial time algorithm for \textit{monotone} valuations that achieves $\frac{1}{2}$-EF and ex-post EFX-with-charity. For \textit{subadditive} valuations, we achieve ex-ante $\frac{1}{3}$-EF and ex-post $\frac{1}{2}$-EFX.
item.dc:creator: Telikepalli Kavitha, Surya Panchapakesan, Rohit Vaish, Vignesh Viswanathan, Jatin Yadav

item.title: Almost Sharp Equivalence between Approximate Message Passing and Low-Degree Polynomials
item.description: arXiv:2609.06988v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We prove a sharp lower bound for growing-degree polynomial estimation in the symmetric rank-one matrix estimation problem. The observation is \[ \boldsymbol{Y}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \boldsymbol{\theta} \boldsymbol{\theta}^{\top}+\boldsymbol{W}, \] where the coordinates of $\boldsymbol{\theta}$ are independent with a common, fixed sub-Gaussian distribution $\pi_\Theta$ satisfying $\mathbb E[\Theta]\neq0$, and $\boldsymbol{W}$ is symmetric with independent standard Gaussian upper-triangular entries. For every such prior, we give an explicit finite-dimensional bound implying that every sequence of polynomial estimators of degree $D(n)=o(n^{1/60})$ has normalized mean-square error with limit inferior at least $\mathbb E[\Theta^2]-q_{\mathsf{amp}}$, the limiting error of Bayes approximate message passing (AMP). This extends the constant-degree equivalence of Montanari and Wein~\cite{montanari2025equivalence} to growing degree under the same prior assumptions. Combined with their polynomial approximation of fixed-iteration AMP, the bound identifies the exact limiting low-degree MMSE whenever $D(n)\to\infty$ within this range. It thereby answers the growing-degree AMP-equivalence question discussed in~\cite{wein2025computational, maleki2026high} for nonzero-mean sub-Gaussian priors in the stated degree range. We also obtain a moment-dependent finite-dimensional lower bound for any nonzero-mean prior with all moments finite. The proof bounds low-degree MMSE using \emph{conditional} joint cumulants and a refined application of Jensen's inequality. The conditional cumulants are defined using an auxiliary Gaussian channel $\boldsymbol{R}$ calibrated to the AMP fixed point. This retains signal dependence that is lost in unconditional cumulant bounds and produces the cancellations needed for quantitative control as the degree grows.
item.dc:creator: Zhangsong Li
